newsitem.title: JAPAN: Asian crude oil prices seen firm in the long term.
newsitem.headline: Asian crude oil prices seen firm in the long term.

text.p: Crude prices were steady in Asia on Friday as most traders here saw the tumble in oil prices overnight as a brief phenomenon in a fundamentally firm market.

Oil prices plummeted on overseas markets as traders rushed to sell heating oil futures, continuing the profit-taking triggered on Wednesday when the American Petroleum Institute reported a larger-than-expected buildup in distillate stocks, including heating oil.
A rumour in New York, later dismissed, that Saudi Arabia supported a higher output ceiling for the Organisation of Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) also trimmed crude prices.
Traders in Asia saw the decline as a temporary, saying that fundamentals for heating oil were strong, given the approach of winter in the northern hemisphere.
They said this meant oil prices were also likely to be strong as crude prices had recently looked to the oil products market for direction.
"I think the crude oil market will be fairly stable," a dealer with a trading company said.
"For the time being, that (product price decline) is the biggest reason for crude's dive," he said.
The approach of winter and generally low stocks of oil products in the West were the strongest reasons for believing oil product prices would be steady, traders said.
As if to support the argument, indications for benchmark crude oil prices showed a recovery during Asian trading hours.
The benchmark U.S. light crude oil for November delivery had dipped 81 cents to close at $24.26 per barrel on Thursday.
However, by late morning trade in Tokyo on Friday, the November contract traded six cents higher at $24.32 per barrel on the after-hours ACCESS system.

The November futures contract for North Sea Brent, a global benchmark, on the Singapore International Monetary Exchange (SIMEX) had not been traded by Tokyo midday on Friday, but was quoted at $23.58/23.75 per barrel.
The level was almost unchanged from the contract's close at $23.58 per barrel on London's International Petroleum Exchange (IPE) on Thursday.
The close on the IPE was just four cents above the session's low and down 69 cents from the previous day.

Some traders said the overnight fall in crude prices was also part of a cyclical pattern in the market, and that participants would buy to hunt bargains in a weak market and sell to take profits in a strong market.
"Unless there's some fresh bearish news I believe it's going to be cyclical, and we'll see a repetition of the same pattern of rises and falls," a broker said.

Crude oil prices have been on an upward trend for most of this year on the back of firm demand and tensions in the Middle East. Traders have also been reluctant to sell oil while stock levels are low.
Some traders attributed the overnight dip to a technical correction to the rise in crude oil prices earlier in the week.
On Tuesday, the November Brent contract reached a contract high of $24.70 on the IPE, the highest level there since the Gulf War ended in February 1991.
"Definitely it (Thursday's dip) was partly a reaction to the recent increase," the Western dealer said.
